solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Urban-dweller's private during relationship

indicators.note: something happening during a period sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a tie is a bond or connection between people
your own things are private to you

explanation.surface: Gossip about a city-dweller keeping something private within a relationship.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay: OWN goes inside TIE.
explanation.definitionFit: A townie is an informal, slightly dismissive term for someone who lives in a town or city rather than the countryside.

clue.text: Some of church, having time, organised Harvest Festival season?

parts.note: T is the standard abbreviation for time
to run an event is to organise it
harvest festivals are traditionally held in September, abbreviated Sept

explanation.surface: A parish church planning its Harvest Festival celebrations in good time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Organised' looks like an anagram signal but is simply RAN. Harvest Festival is the British church thanksgiving for the crops, held around late September.
explanation.definitionFit: A transept is one of the two arms crossing the nave of a cross-shaped church building, so it forms part of it.

clue.text: Robust male tucking into pasty needs salt

indicators.note: food tucked into goes inside the eater, so one piece is placed within another

parts.note: pasty here is the adjective: pale, wan
hale means healthy and strong
M is the abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: A hearty man eating a pasty who wants salt to go with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pasty' reads as the British baked pastry, but it is the adjective meaning pale. 'Salt' is crossword shorthand for an old sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: An old salt is a seasoned sailor, and a whaleman is a sailor serving on a whaling ship.

clue.text: Regularly nibbled by goat

indicators.note: something done regularly happens at even intervals, so every other letter is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters
by as in multiplication, three by four, written with the times sign X

explanation.surface: Something being nibbled at steadily by a goat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' looks like a passive 'nibbled by', but it is the multiplication sign X.
explanation.definitionFit: The ibex is a wild mountain goat of the Alps and Asia with long curved horns.

clue.text: Exclusive group of people governing stylish private hospital

indicators.note: a body made of its members holds them inside, so one part is placed within the other

parts.note: a clique is a small exclusive circle
the party in power is said to be in

explanation.surface: An elite circle running a fashionable private clinic.
explanation.walkthrough: The French spelling suits the 'stylish' tag: a smart private clinic.
explanation.definitionFit: Clinique is the French word for a clinic, used in English for a fashionable private medical establishment.

clue.text: Barking at Cecil, akita wants large amount of water

indicators.note: barking is British slang for mad, and mad letters fall into disorder

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A dog barking at a man called Cecil because it is thirsty.
explanation.walkthrough: An akita is a Japanese dog breed, so 'Barking' looks literal; it is the British slang for crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Lake Titicaca, on the border of Peru and Bolivia, is the largest lake in South America, a vast body of fresh water.

clue.text: Plain-spoken, unfinished sonnet twice broadcast

indicators.note: something left unfinished is missing its end, so the final letter goes
to broadcast is to scatter widely, as seed is sown, so the letters are strewn into a new order

parts.note: the poem without its last letter
the same letters a second time

explanation.surface: A blunt poet's half-done sonnet being read out on air twice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' suggests radio, but here it means scattered.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-nonsense person is direct and businesslike, speaking frankly without frills, which is what plain-spoken means.

clue.text: Maybe member of crocodile viewable by all in unusual environment

indicators.note: an environment is what surrounds something, so one piece is enclosed by the other

parts.note: queer in its old sense of odd or strange
U is the British film certificate for universal viewing

explanation.surface: A zoo crocodile, visible to all visitors, living in an odd enclosure.
explanation.walkthrough: A crocodile in British usage is a line of schoolchildren walking in pairs, so its members are queuing, not reptiles. U is the film rating suitable for everyone.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone standing in a long orderly line of children, a crocodile, is one example of a person waiting in a queue.

clue.text: Fake European art's strangely variable

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for European

indicators.note: acting strangely means behaving out of the normal order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored
in algebra x, y and z are the usual unknown variables

explanation.surface: A forged piece of European art whose quality varies oddly.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's of art's is just part of the fodder, giving the S.
explanation.definitionFit: Ersatz, borrowed from German, describes an inferior imitation or substitute, something not genuine.

clue.text: Stir partly created by one Kawasaki doing a U-turn

indicators.note: a U-turn sends a vehicle back the way it came, so the letters run backwards
only part of the phrase is needed, so the letters lie inside the words

parts.note: the run of letters spanning the two words

explanation.surface: A commotion caused by a motorcyclist turning a Kawasaki round in the road.
explanation.walkthrough: Kawasaki is a motorbike maker, which makes the U-turn look literal.
explanation.definitionFit: To stir someone is to rouse them from sleep, and awaken is a direct synonym of rouse.

clue.text: Like a particular sausage link chopped into four quarters

indicators.note: going into something means ending up inside it

parts.note: the compass points are the quarters; here south, east, south, south

indicators.note: chopping cuts something up into a jumble, so its letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A sausage link being chopped into four pieces in the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Link' sits naturally with sausages, but it is the fodder. Compass points stand for quarters; the setter picks whichever letters are needed.
explanation.definitionFit: Some sausages are sold without a casing, and these are known in shops as skinless sausages.

clue.text: Errors serving large drink terribly fast inhibiting university student

parts.note: a double is a twice-sized measure of spirits

indicators.note: to inhibit is to hold back or restrain, so one piece holds others within it
done terribly means done badly and out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
U is the abbreviation for university
L for learner, as on British learner-driver plates

explanation.surface: A university student drinking heavily and quickly, making mistakes as a waiter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Serving' suggests a waiter with drinks, but it is the tennis serve. L stands for a learner, so any student.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis a double fault is two failed serves in a row, so these are mistakes made while serving.

clue.text: Take action against unknown in mid-50s, the centre of a crisis

definitions.text: in mid-50s, the centre of a crisis

parts.note: to sue is to take legal action against someone
z is one of the algebraic unknowns

explanation.surface: Taking legal action over some unidentified crisis back in the 1950s.
explanation.walkthrough: The Suez Crisis of 1956 saw Britain and France invade Egypt over the canal and then withdraw under international pressure.
explanation.definitionFit: The Suez Canal was the place at the heart of the 1956 international crisis, so it was the centre of that crisis.

clue.text: Group of people trace books on criminal

indicators.note: in an across answer, putting one thing on another places it after, so the order is swapped

parts.note: a con is a convict
a tinge is a slight trace of colour
NT is the New Testament, a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A gang tracing the account books of a crook.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'on' places what comes before after what follows, so the criminal comes first.
explanation.definitionFit: A contingent is a group of people sharing a common origin or purpose, forming part of a larger gathering.

clue.text: Bedding, light, and the rest, taken through Channel port

indicators.note: whatever is taken through a place passes inside it, so the outer piece holds the others

parts.note: Dover is the English port on the Channel, facing France
UV is ultraviolet light
etc stands for et cetera, and the rest

explanation.surface: A list of luggage, bedding, lamps and so on, carried through a ferry port.
explanation.walkthrough: The commas make it look like a packing list, but they only separate the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A duvet cover is the removable fabric case for a quilt, and so counts as an item of bedding.

clue.text: Elvis favourite? A tune played in empty pub, say

indicators.note: an emptied thing has lost its contents, so only the outside letters remain
something in a place is inside it

parts.note: the word with its middle removed

indicators.note: music that is played can be improvised freely, so the letters are put into a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
to utter is to say

explanation.surface: An Elvis hit being played on the jukebox in a deserted pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Elvis favourite' suggests a song, but Presley famously loved fried peanut butter and banana sandwiches.
explanation.definitionFit: Elvis Presley's well-known taste for peanut butter sandwiches makes the spread a food he loved, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Air soldier with Forces getting in fuel

parts.note: a para is a paratrooper, dropped from the air
F is force; two of them make FF
taken as written

explanation.surface: A paratrooper with the armed forces taking on fuel supplies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Forces' looks like the armed forces, but it is the physics abbreviation F, doubled.
explanation.definitionFit: Paraffin is the British name for kerosene, an oil burnt in heaters and lamps and used as jet fuel.

clue.text: Swerve to maintain intense turning — in this sport?

indicators.note: to maintain is to hold or keep, so the outer piece holds the other

parts.note: to sway is to swing or veer

indicators.note: something turning faces the other way, so its letters run backwards

parts.note: deep feelings are intense ones

explanation.surface: Swerving while turning hard, as riders do in a particular sport.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes the sport, which is why the definition is just 'this sport'.
explanation.definitionFit: Speedway is motorcycle racing round an oval dirt track, where riders slide and swerve through every turn.

clue.text: English actor moving centre stage, finally, to make an impression

indicators.note: things moving shift position, so these letters change places

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the closing letter is kept

parts.note: the word's last letter
to stamp is to press a mark into something

explanation.surface: An actor taking centre stage at last to make his mark.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Centre stage' reads as a theatre phrase, but the words are split: one is fodder and the other gives only its final letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Terence Stamp was a London-born film actor, known for Billy Budd, Superman II and The Limey.

clue.text: Having seen cuckoo, Edward behaved like a twitcher?

parts.note: a cuckoo is a fool, as is a jerk
Ed is short for Edward

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher named Edward spotting a cuckoo.
explanation.walkthrough: A twitcher is a keen birdwatcher, which fits the cuckoo, but here it means someone who twitches.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who twitches moves with sudden involuntary spasms, which is what jerked describes.

clue.text: Bent sports official on side of Liverpool once

parts.note: a ref is a referee

indicators.note: a side is an edge, so a single outer letter is kept

parts.note: the word's opening letter
ex means former, as once does

explanation.surface: A corrupt referee taking a bribe from a former Liverpool side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent' as British slang for corrupt joins with the referee in the surface; here it means curved back. 'Side' wants to be a team, but marks the edge letter.
explanation.definitionFit: In botany and anatomy reflex describes something turned or folded backwards, as a reflex angle exceeds a straight line.

clue.text: Toss-up just before tea, then next cricket event starts

parts.note: even in the sense of fair or equal
cha is British slang for tea

indicators.note: starts are beginnings, so each word gives only its opening letter

parts.note: the first letters of the three words

explanation.surface: The coin toss at a cricket match, just before the tea interval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Toss-up' suggests the cricket toss but is the definition; 'just before' is not one unit but JUST plus a placing word.
explanation.definitionFit: A toss-up is a situation where either outcome is equally likely, a fifty-fifty probability.

clue.text: Ornamental stone jars dear with fifty percent off

indicators.note: half price removes half, so each word loses its second half

parts.note: the word's first half
the word's first half

explanation.surface: Decorative jars that were expensive, now sold at half price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dear' means expensive in British English, so the half-price sale fits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Jade is a hard green gemstone carved into jewellery and ornaments since ancient times.

clue.text: Discussed crucial landing-place

indicators.note: what is discussed is spoken about, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

parts.note: key means crucial or vital

explanation.walkthrough: 'Discussed crucial' reads as a talking point, but signals a sound match.
explanation.definitionFit: A quay is a stone or concrete platform beside water where boats tie up and unload.

clue.text: Amount of energy left over, playing football perhaps in Scottish outfit

indicators.note: to be in clothing is to be wrapped by it, so the wearer sits inside

parts.note: the kilt is Scottish Highland dress
L is the abbreviation for left
O for over, the cricket scoring abbreviation
v for versus, as in one team playing another in a fixture
a ball is round, like the letter O

explanation.surface: A footballer in a kilt with some energy still to spare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Playing football' looks like one idea, but splits into the fixture's v and a round ball.
explanation.definitionFit: A kilovolt is a unit of electrical potential, loosely a measure of energy; the setter treats it as an amount.

clue.text: Laugh loudly, gorging stuffed prawns in essence repeatedly

indicators.note: the essence of a thing is its core, and repeatedly applies that to each word in turn

parts.note: the single central letter of this seven-letter word, picked out by the middle selection
the central three letters
the central two letters

explanation.surface: Roaring with laughter while greedily eating stuffed prawns.
explanation.walkthrough: The middles are of varying length, taken from three words in a row.
explanation.definitionFit: A guffaw is a loud hearty burst of laughter, and as a verb means to laugh boisterously.

clue.text: Type of sugar daughter passed on to recycle store

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for daughter

indicators.note: recycled material is broken down and remade, so these letters are reformed

parts.note: ex means former, no longer present
taken as written

explanation.surface: A daughter handing sugar on to a recycling store.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Passed on' suggests handing something over, but here it means gone, former.
explanation.definitionFit: Dextrose is the common name for glucose in its natural right-handed form, a simple sugar.

clue.text: Olympic venue to be completed within two years, son recalled

indicators.note: to recall is to call back, so the letters go back the other way
within means inside, so one piece sits in the other

parts.note: Y is the abbreviation for year, twice
the end is what remains to be completed
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: An Olympic stadium that must be finished within two years.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole string is reversed once the son is added at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Sydney, Australia hosted the Summer Olympic Games in 2000.
